summary: Specifies requirements for Delegated Path Validation (DPV) and Delegated Path Discovery (DPD) of public key certificates, which let a client hand certificate-checking work to a server. It also specifies requirements for managing the policies they use.

plainLanguage.summary: Checking that a digital ID is trustworthy takes work. This document lists what is needed so a small device can ask a helper server to do the checking.

questions: how can a server validate certificate chains for a client
how can a server validate certificates for a client
why would a device use dpv or dpd
subtitle: Requirements for letting servers validate certificates and collect certificate information on behalf of clients.

tldr.problem: Validating digital certificates is computationally expensive and time-consuming, and small devices may lack the processing power or network connectivity to do it themselves.
tldr.mechanism: Delegated Path Validation (DPV) lets a client hand off certificate validation to a trusted server, while Delegated Path Discovery (DPD) lets a server collect certificate chain and revocation information that the client validates locally.
tldr.outcome: Both services reduce processing burden on constrained devices and allow centralized management of certificate validation policies in enterprises.

today: RFC 3379 is an Informational document that specifies requirements for DPV and DPD protocols. These requirements have guided the development of certificate validation and discovery protocols used in PKI systems, particularly for constrained devices and enterprise environments requiring centralized validation policies.

sections.title: The Certificate Validation Challenge
sections.content:
Validating a digital certificate requires checking a certification path that may contain multiple certificates linked together, starting with an end-entity certificate and ending with a trusted root. The validation process must fetch these certificates, obtain revocation information such as CRLs or OCSP responses, perform signature verification on each certificate, and apply policy constraints. This is computationally expensive and requires network access to multiple repositories.

Constrained devices like mobile phones and PDAs face a fundamental problem: they may lack sufficient memory, processing power, or network bandwidth to perform complete certification path validation. Even devices with adequate processing power may want to reduce latency by offloading this work to a trusted server. Additionally, enterprises often want to manage certificate validation policies centrally, applying consistent validation rules across all clients.

This document specifies requirements for two related services: Delegated Path Validation (DPV) for server-side certificate validation, and Delegated Path Discovery (DPD) for server-side collection of certificate information that clients validate locally.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking if a digital ID is real takes a lot of work and smarts. Small devices might not be able to do it. This explains how a server can help.

sections.title: Delegated Path Validation (DPV)
sections.content:
Delegated Path Validation allows a server to perform real-time certificate validation on behalf of a client. The client sends a certificate and receives a response indicating whether it is valid, invalid, or unknown according to a validation policy. The server constructs the certification path, obtains revocation status information, and applies validation rules.

DPV is valuable for several reasons. Constrained execution environments like telephones and PDAs may lack the memory or processing power for complete PKIX-compliant path validation. In applications where minimum latency is critical, delegating validation to a trusted server can be faster than the client performing path discovery and validation itself, even accounting for network communication time. The processing overhead of signature verification for each certificate in a long path can exceed the delay of communicating with a server.

Another key benefit: DPV enables centralized management of validation policies. Clients can direct the server to perform path validation according to a particular validation policy, ensuring consistency across an enterprise. A client that trusts a DPV server can rely on that server to maintain centralized records of validation activities for audit and compliance purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: You send the ID to a smart helper server that says 'yes, that is real' or 'no, something is wrong.' The server does all the hard checking work. An office can tell all its helper servers to check the same way.

sections.title: Delegated Path Discovery (DPD)
sections.content:
Delegated Path Discovery serves clients that want to perform path validation themselves but need help gathering the necessary data. A DPD server collects certificates, CRLs, delta CRLs, and OCSP responses from multiple repositories, then returns them to the client for local validation.

The client is spared the complexity of interacting with diverse repository systems accessed via different protocols like LDAP, HTTP, or FTP. A single query to the DPD server can replace multiple repository queries, and the server's caching can reduce latency. Importantly, since certificates and revocation information are digitally signed, the client need not trust the DPD server to the same extent as a DPV server; the client only needs to trust that the server returns current information available to it.

DPD is especially valuable for clients that do much of the PKI processing themselves and simply want a server to handle data acquisition. This allows clients to maintain local control over policy decisions while benefiting from the server's direct access to certificate repositories.
sections.plainLanguage: The server gathers all the papers about the ID from different places and hands them to you. Then you check the papers yourself. You do not have to trust the server as much because the papers have signatures on them.

sections.title: DPV Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
The DPV protocol must allow clients to request validation according to a specific validation policy. If the server does not support the requested policy, it must return an error. The server MUST determine whether the certificate is valid, invalid, unknown, or whether validity could not be determined due to an error.

The server must support validation at a time other than the current time, allowing clients to check whether a certificate was valid at a specific moment in the past. The server MUST obtain revocation status information for that validation time. If revocation status information is unavailable for the requested time, the server MUST indicate that the certificate is invalid.

The DPV response MUST be bound to the DPV request so the client can verify that all request parameters were considered. This can be accomplished by including a one-way hash of the request in the response. Additionally, the response MUST be authenticated and digitally signed, so the client can prove to third parties that the validation was performed by the expected server. The protocol MUST prevent replay attacks without relying on synchronized clocks.

The client must be able to request that the server include additional information in the response, such as the certification path, revocation status information, or time-stamp tokens, allowing relying parties not trusting the DPV server to independently verify the validation result.
sections.plainLanguage: The server follows rules: check at the time you ask, say what went wrong if the ID is bad, sign the answer so you know it came from the server, and prove you really checked.

sections.title: Validation and Discovery Policies
sections.content:
A validation policy is a set of rules against which certificate validation is performed. It includes trust anchors (the root certificates the client trusts), revocation requirements (whether to use CRLs, OCSP responses, or delta CRLs), and end-entity certificate specific requirements such as mandatory certificate extensions or name forms.

For DPV, the policy defines how the server constructs the path, what revocation information sources to use, and what constraints must be satisfied. For DPD, a path discovery policy is a subset of a validation policy that focuses on the discovery criteria. Since the DPD client performs local validation, it can apply additional selection criteria to paths returned by the server; therefore, a simpler discovery policy can be used.

Policies may be complex and allow for parameter settings, but clients typically reference a standard validation policy for their application or accept the server's default policy. The policy must ensure that at least one valid certification path exists between the end-entity certificate and a trust anchor, with no expired or revoked certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say which root IDs to trust, whether to check if the ID got cancelled, and what extra details the ID needs to have. Different offices can use different rules.

sections.title: Trust and Security Issues
sections.content:
A DPV client must fully trust the DPV server, as much as it would trust its own path validation software. The server's positive response carries the weight of the server's reputation. However, different DPV clients may trust different servers, and not all servers will convince all relying parties.

Clients operating under an organizational validation policy must ensure that each trusted DPV server operates under that same policy. When no policy reference is present in the DPV request, the client should verify that the server's chosen policy is appropriate.

The revocation status information obtained is for a specific validation time, which may differ from the time a digital signature was created. The DPV client ought to adjust the validation time to account for the lag between key compromise and detection, reporting of compromise, revocation authority processing, and revocation information distribution. There is no specific confidentiality requirement within the protocol itself, but confidentiality can be achieved using lower-layer security protocols when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: You have to trust the server. The server has to check things the same way your organization wants. There is a delay between when something goes wrong and when everyone knows about it.
